children.text: It's Tuesday, the monthly close is still open, and the site lead is holding three problems at once. A suite is mid-move-out, a third-floor resident has no hot water, and the water bill is well above last month with no change in occupancy to explain it. Leasing can fill the unit. Maintenance can get the boiler back. Neither task tells you whether the extra water is a leak, a common-area load, or a charge you can't defend on paper.

That split is the heart of multifamily property management. Occupancy and repairs keep the building open. Utility data, fair charges, and leak response decide whether bulk utilities sit inside operating expenses or get split in a way a resident can check.

How a Multifamily Community Actually Runs

children.text: Three money paths run through every property, a 12-suite walk-up and a large stacked building alike.
The building pays one bill.

On a master-metered property the utility sends a single invoice. You then decide how much, if any, comes back from residents. Recover nothing, and the full amount stays in operating expenses even when suites sit empty.

Unit meters make the leftover visible.

A
master meter
is the utility's meter for the whole building. A
unit meter
measures one suite, or one defined load, so resident use can be separated from what the building itself burns.

Bulk utilities compress net operating income because the expense hits the statement whether occupancy is full or not. Estimated allocations then create disputes, and leasing staff inherit the argument at renewal. The walk-up and the tower share the same three paths. Build the inventory.

California's
official landlord-tenant guidance

says landlords cannot charge more than the actual utility cost and must disclose how water charges are calculated when tenants are billed through a submeter. State law also requires itemized master-meter electricity or gas billing, including meter readings, applicable rates, and quantities attributable to rate blocks.
Charge
Resident must see

The first invoice is the fairness test

Owners often pay for the equipment while residents keep the lower bill. Households that are already stretched will judge the program by this month's charge, not by a saving that shows up over years. Publish the method. Put hardship and correction rules in the lease addendum. Don't launch a new charge that spikes a low-income household's first invoice. A conservation change that raises the immediate bill will stall, even if the annual total would have dropped.
Vendor Coordination Without Losing the Week

Treat the crew as a relay, not a phone list. On a utility project the usual cast is the property manager, the site superintendent, a licensed electrician, a plumber, and the metering contractor. Each person should leave with one job finished and the next person able to start.
The manager sets the loads.
Say which meters must be separated, which suites can be entered, and which common rooms stay off the resident bill. If that brief is vague, the trades will meter whatever is easy to reach.
The superintendent books access.
One or two days per stack beats weeks of open units. Residents get a notice with a date, a window, and a contact. Keys, pets, and occupied bedrooms are planned before the van arrives.
The electrician or plumber installs to the approved design.
They don't invent a new one on the ladder. Mixed tariffs, a boiler room, and a house panel each need a labelled point.
The metering firm commissions.
Meters have to talk to the billing file before anyone signs off. A meter that reads on a handheld and never reaches the invoice is not finished work.

Before work starts, demand proof of insurance and bonding, a unit-access plan, the resident notice, a named site lead, and a punch list tied to payment. Hold the last draw until the punch list is closed. A crew that is paid in full on the install day has little reason to come back for a dead meter.

Three buildings change the paperwork, not the relay. A mixed-use property may need commercial and residential reads on different tariffs, so don't put a shop and a suite on the same rate block. A condominium or strata needs the corporation or council to authorise entry and billing before anyone drills. A five-to-ten-unit building still needs the same insurance, notice, and punch list, even though the site day is short.
If the vendor leaves tomorrow, the owner should still hold meter IDs, as-built locations, and a support number.
That file is the control test. Photos of the panel help, but they don't replace an ID that matches the billing account. Coordinate the site day through a clear scope for
utility metering installation and maintenance
, then keep the as-builts with the property, not only in the contractor's inbox.

children.text: What the turnkey column looks like in practice

Take Axis Meter Solutions as the worked example of that right-hand column, not as a slogan. Equipment, install, commissioning, tenant billing, and service sit in one program. Owners pay no upfront capital. The provider owns and maintains the gear on a standard 20-year term. A typical path from agreement to live meters is 8 to 10 weeks, including equipment lead time, with on-site access often limited to one or two days.

Electricity, water, gas where it's permitted, thermal energy, and common-area meters can be scoped together. Water installs include leak and flood sensors at no added charge. In Ontario, electricity unit submetering is done under Ontario Energy Board licence ES-2022-0268, and equipment is chosen to meet Measurement Canada or U.S. rules before kickoff. The same pattern covers buildings of about 5 to 10 units and larger portfolios across Canada and the United States.
A long agreement swaps capital and staffing for a contracted operating cost. It's a poor fit if the owner wants to self-perform billing and already has licensed in-house metering staff.

If your team can replace failed meters, explain rate blocks, and keep the audit file for a decade, stay in the left column. If that work would land on the same person who already runs leasing and turns, the right column is the lighter operating load. The next section is the fork, not another list of features.
